title: Constraint satisfaction by backtracking

problem.name: Constraint satisfaction
problem.statement_latex:
For variables $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in[d]$ and explicitly given constraints $C_1,\ldots,C_m$, find $x\in[d]^n$ with $\bigwedge_jC_j(x)=1$, or decide unsatisfiability. Assume a classical branching rule and a predicate that rejects inconsistent partial assignments. Let $T$ be the size of their backtracking tree and $D\leq n$ its depth.
The tree comparison counts branching and predicate-oracle calls, while the explicit bounded-arity comparison uses quantum gates and classical bit operations.

quantum.headline_latex: $O(\sqrt{TD})$ detection queries and $O(\sqrt T D^{3/2}\log D)$ witness queries, Montanaro's quantum backtracking.
quantum.headline_text: $O(\sqrt{TD})$ detection queries and $O(\sqrt T D^{3/2}\log D)$ witness queries, Montanaro's quantum backtracking.
quantum.details_latex: These are constant-error bounds for the supplied branching rule and pruning predicate. Reversible implementation costs multiply the query count. The quantum walk explores the same partial-assignment tree as the specified classical backtracking procedure; its depth dependence is explicit in the bounds.
quantum.details_text: These are constant-error bounds for the supplied branching rule and pruning predicate. Reversible implementation costs multiply the query count. classical.headline_latex: $O(T)$ tree queries, depth-first backtracking; $2^{o(n)}\operatorname{poly}(n,m)$ bit operations, Boolean tensor contraction for fixed domain and arity.
classical.headline_text: $O(T)$ tree queries, depth-first backtracking; $2^{o(n)}\operatorname{poly}(n,m)$ bit operations, Boolean tensor contraction for fixed domain and arity.
classical.details_latex: For fixed domain $d$ and arity $r$, the time bound is $\operatorname{poly}(n,m)2^{O_{d,r}(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}$. Encoding each variable in $O(\log d)$ bits and forbidding disallowed local assignments produces a fixed-width CNF with $O(n)$ variables. Exact counting and self-reduction decide feasibility and recover a witness in polynomial space. When $m=O(n)$, the exponent improves to $O_{d,r}(n/\sqrt{\log n})$. The tree-query comparison remains useful for an instance whose pruning rules yield a small $T$; the bounded-arity expression is the unrestricted explicit-input comparator in that regime.

strength.description_latex: Nearly quadratic in the size of a specified search tree, through a quantum walk. Fixed-domain, fixed-arity instances also admit the displayed subexponential classical bound, whose exponent has no power saving.
strength.description_text: Nearly quadratic in the size of a specified search tree, through a quantum walk. Fixed-domain, fixed-arity instances also admit the displayed subexponential classical bound, whose exponent has no power saving.

evidence.description_latex: Rigorous acceleration of the supplied backtracking procedure; evidence against unrestricted classical solvers depends on the constraint language and instances.

hardware.description_latex: A path requires $O(D\log d)$ qubits, together with reversible constraint-evaluation and phase-estimation workspace. The register count is polynomial, while a tree of exponential size entails exponentially many coherent walk operations. Useful large instances require fault tolerance.

algorithm_items.content_latex: \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.02374}{Montanaro, \emph{Quantum Walk Speedup of Backtracking Algorithms} (Theory of Computing 2018)}. Theorems 1--2; Algorithm 1 defines classical backtracking, Algorithm 2 defines quantum detection, and the section on finding a marked vertex gives witness recovery.
